What broader lesson does Bacon's essay convey about the role of studies?
questions.answer: Studies shape our character and cure the defects of the mind, just as exercise cures the body. Used in the right measure and checked by experience, they make us wise, able and balanced.

questions.q: What are the three uses of studies?
questions.answer: Studies serve for delight in private and in retirement, for ornament in conversation, and for ability in judging and managing business.

questions.q: Why does Bacon compare natural abilities to natural plants?
questions.answer: Just as plants need pruning to grow well, our natural talents need to be trimmed and shaped by study. Study improves raw abilities, and experience in turn corrects study.

questions.q: How should we read, according to Bacon?
questions.answer: Not to contradict others, nor to believe everything blindly, nor merely to find things to talk about, but to weigh and consider what we read.

questions.q: Explain: 'Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.'
questions.answer: Some books need to be read only in parts, some read quickly without close attention, and a few important ones read fully, carefully and thoughtfully so that we absorb them.

questions.q: How do reading, conference and writing help a man?
questions.answer: Reading fills the mind with knowledge, conference (discussion) makes one quick and ready in reply, and writing makes one exact and precise. Without them one needs a great memory, a present wit or cunning.

questions.q: How can different defects of the mind be cured by studies, according to Bacon?
questions.answer: Bacon says every impediment of the mind can be removed by a fitting study, as exercises cure bodily ills. A wandering mind should study mathematics, one who cannot distinguish should study the schoolmen, and one who cannot argue should study lawyers' cases.

questions.q: Comment on Bacon's style in 'Of Studies'.
questions.answer: His style is aphoristic: short, balanced, pithy sentences that pack much wisdom into few words, such as 'Reading maketh a full man'. He uses similes and metaphors (plants, tasting books) and parallel structure, and many lines have become proverbs.

or.q: What, according to Bacon, are the dangers of excessive study?
or.answer: Too much study is sloth, making one lazy. Using learning too much for show is affectation, and judging everything only by bookish rules is the whim of a scholar. Study must be balanced and corrected by experience.

questions.q: 'Histories make men wise; poets witty …' Explain.
questions.answer: Bacon says each subject develops a quality: history gives wisdom through lessons of the past, poetry wit, mathematics subtlety, natural philosophy depth, moral philosophy seriousness, and logic and rhetoric the power to argue. What we study passes into our character.
